q: how to create a new branch in git
git create branch command
how to switch branches in git
git branch checkout example
git create and switch to branch
a: Use `git branch <name>` to create a new branch at the current commit. Use `git switch <name>` (Git 2.23+) or `git checkout <name>` to switch. Combine both with `git switch -c <name>` or `git checkout -b <name>`. Branch names should be descriptive and use hyphens (e.g., `feature/add-auth`). List branches with `git branch` (local) or `git branch -a` (all, including remotes).
code:
# Create a new branch (stays on current branch)
git branch feature/login

# Switch to branch (Git 2.23+)
git switch feature/login

# Create and switch in one command
git switch -c feature/login
# Legacy equivalent:
git checkout -b feature/login

# List branches
git branch
# * feature/login
#   main

git branch -a  # includes remote branches

# Rename a branch (while on it)
git branch -m feature-login

# Delete a branch (merged)
git branch -d feature/login

# Delete a branch (force, even if unmerged)
git branch -D feature/login

q: how to merge branches in git
git merge example
how to merge branch into main git
git merge vs rebase
how to merge feature branch to main
a: `git merge` integrates changes from one branch into another. First, switch to the target branch (e.g., `main`), then run `git merge <source-branch>`. Git creates a merge commit that has two parents, preserving the full history of both branches. Use `--no-ff` to force a merge commit even for fast-forward merges. Merge conflicts happen when both branches modify the same lines — resolve them manually, stage, then commit.
code:
# Merge feature branch into main
git switch main
git merge feature/login

# With a merge commit message
git merge feature/login -m "Merge login feature into main"

# Force non-fast-forward merge (preserves branch history)
git merge --no-ff feature/login

# Abort a merge if conflicts are too complex
git merge --abort

# After resolving conflicts:
git add .
git merge --continue
# Or: git commit (without --continue in older versions)

# View merge history
git log --graph --oneline --all

# Integration flow example:
# git switch main
# git pull origin main           # update main
# git switch -c feature/new-feature
# ... work, commit, work, commit ...
# git switch main
# git pull origin main           # get latest
# git merge feature/new-feature
# git push origin main

q: how to rebase in git
git rebase explained
git rebase vs merge
how to rebase branch onto main
git interactive rebase example
how to squash commits with rebase
a: Rebasing rewrites commit history by applying commits from one branch onto the tip of another. Unlike merging (which creates a merge commit), rebase produces a linear history. Use `git rebase main` while on your feature branch to replay your commits after the latest main commits. Interactive rebase (`git rebase -i HEAD~n`) lets you squash, reorder, reword, or drop commits. Never rebase shared/public branches — it rewrites history and causes issues for collaborators.
code:
# Rebase feature branch onto latest main
git switch feature/login
git rebase main

# Interactive rebase for last 3 commits
git rebase -i HEAD~3
# Editor opens with:
# pick abc123 First commit
# pick def456 Second commit
# pick 789ghi Third commit
# Change 'pick' to:
#   squash (s) - combine with previous commit
#   reword (r) - change commit message
#   fixup (f) - combine, discard message
#   edit (e) - stop to amend
#   drop (d) - delete commit

# Rebase onto specific branch
git rebase origin/main

# Continue after resolving conflicts
git rebase --continue

# Skip a problematic commit
git rebase --skip

# Abort rebase entirely
git rebase --abort

# Config: auto-stash before rebase
git config --global rebase.autoStash true

q: how to resolve merge conflicts in git
git merge conflict resolution
how to fix merge conflicts git
git conflict markers explained
how to resolve git conflicts in vscode
a: Merge conflicts occur when two branches modify the same part of a file. Git marks conflicts in the file with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers. The section between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is your current branch's version; between `=======` and `>>>>>>> theirs` is the incoming branch's version. Manually edit to keep the correct code (or a mix of both), remove the conflict markers, then `git add` the resolved file and `git merge --continue`.
code:
# Scenario: merging feature into main causes conflict

# File with conflict markers (_index.html_):
# <<<<<<< HEAD (current: main)
# <title>My Site</title>
# =======
# <title>My Awesome Site</title>
# >>>>>>> feature/update-title

# Steps to resolve:
# 1. Open the conflicted file in editor
# 2. Decide which version(s) to keep
# 3. Remove conflict markers
# 4. Result:
# <title>My Awesome Site</title>
# 5. Stage the resolved file
git add index.html

# 6. Continue the merge
git merge --continue
# Or: git commit

# Alternative: accept one side entirely
# Keep current branch version:
git checkout --ours index.html
# Keep incoming branch version:
git checkout --theirs index.html

# See which files are conflicted
git status
# Both modified:   index.html

# Use a merge tool
git mergetool

q: how to create a pull request in git
git pull request workflow
how to push to remote and create PR
git push origin branch example
github pull request how to
a: A pull request (PR) is a review mechanism on platforms like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. The workflow: create a feature branch, make commits, push to remote with `git push origin <branch>`, then open a PR via the platform UI or CLI (e.g., `gh pr create`). Before pushing, ensure your branch is up to date with the target branch via rebase or merge. After the PR is approved and merged, delete the remote branch and clean up locally.
code:
# Full PR workflow example

# 1. Start from up-to-date main
git switch main
git pull origin main

# 2. Create feature branch
git switch -c feature/user-auth

# 3. Work and commit
echo "auth logic" > auth.py
git add auth.py
git commit -m "Add user authentication module"

# 4. Push to remote
git push origin feature/user-auth
# Output: remote: Create a pull request for 'feature/user-auth' on GitHub by visiting:
# remote:   https://github.com/user/repo/pull/new/feature/user-auth

# 5. Using GitHub CLI to create PR
git push origin feature/user-auth
gh pr create --title "Add user authentication" --body "Implements login, signup, and password reset." --base main

# 6. Update PR with more commits
# (just push more commits to the same branch)
echo "tests" > test_auth.py
git add test_auth.py
git commit -m "Add auth tests"
git push origin feature/user-auth  # PR updates automatically

# 7. After PR is merged, clean up
git switch main
git pull origin main
git branch -d feature/user-auth      # delete local
git push origin --delete feature/user-auth  # delete remote

q: how to undo last commit in git
git revert vs reset explained
how to undo changes in git
git reset soft mixed hard
how to unstage a file in git
git discard local changes
a: Git offers several ways to undo changes depending on scope. `git reset` moves the HEAD and optionally the index/working directory: `--soft` (keeps changes staged), `--mixed` (default, unstages changes), `--hard` (discards changes entirely). `git revert` creates a new commit that undoes a previous commit — safe for shared branches. `git restore` unstages or discards working directory changes. Use `git reflog` to recover lost commits after a reset.
code:
# Undo last commit but keep changes staged
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Undo last commit and unstage (keep changes in working dir)
git reset HEAD~1
# or: git reset --mixed HEAD~1

# Undo last commit and discard all changes
# WARNING: this deletes your changes
git reset --hard HEAD~1

# Undo a specific commit safely (creates new commit)
git revert abc123

# Unstage a file (keep working directory changes)
git restore --staged file.py
# or legacy: git reset HEAD file.py

# Discard working directory changes
git restore file.py
# or legacy: git checkout -- file.py

# Undo all local changes (reset to remote)
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main

# View reflog to find lost commits
git reflog
# Then reset to the lost commit:
# git reset --hard HEAD@{2}
